title: What We Believe
description: What you believe about children and families shows up in every decision you make, starting with the first message you send home.
objectives: Define asset-based thinking and contrast it with deficit-based approaches to students and families.
Identify how deficit narratives show up in schools, in language, policy, and practice, and reframe them.
Name how your own background and cultural lens shape what you notice, and describe ways to engage respectfully across difference.
Choose family-partnership actions that treat families as experts on their own children.
Share a student's strengths and areas of growth with a family in plain, strengths-based language, and use what families share to shape classroom decisions.
Connect asset-based mindsets to KIPP DC's mission and your own personal why.

blocks.text: Every teacher holds beliefs about children, whether or not they have ever said them out loud. Some of those beliefs were handed to you by your own schooling, by the media, or by the neighborhood you grew up in. This section helps you name them, check them against research, and turn the ones worth keeping into things you actually do, especially with families.

blocks.title: Your plan for the 65 minutes
blocks.text: Content and required readings (35 min), knowledge check (10), mindset check (5), final task (15). Optional videos, podcasts, and articles are marked and are not part of the time estimate.
Not graded. Rate how much you agree with each statement right now. You will rate the same statements again after the knowledge check, and you can revisit both before your first evaluation period.

statements.text: I start from what a student can already do before I plan support.
Families who seem distant from school still care deeply about their children's education.
I can describe a student's growth area to a family in plain, strengths-based language.

blocks.text: **Asset-based thinking** starts with the strengths, knowledge, and cultural resources children bring into your classroom, rather than starting with what they lack. A child who translates for a grandparent, runs a younger sibling's morning, or knows every bus route in the city already has skills you can teach from. Asset-based thinking does not mean ignoring gaps or lowering the bar. It means beginning from what is there so that you can build toward rigorous work.
The deficit ideology it pushes against

Much of U.S. public education has been shaped by what scholar Paul Gorski calls **deficit ideology**: the belief that low achievement is caused by what students and families lack, such as motivation, language, or values, instead of by the structural inequalities around them (Gorski, 2011). Notice how this connects to Section 1. The story of DC's schools is a story of systems, not of families who did not care.
Why expectations matter

In 1968, Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson told elementary teachers that certain students had been identified as likely to show big intellectual gains. The students had actually been chosen at random. At the end of the year, those students had gained more on a test than their classmates. The finding became known as the **Pygmalion effect**: teacher expectations can work like a self-fulfilling prophecy. (Later research has found that expectation effects are real but usually smaller and less consistent than the original study suggested, which is a good reminder to hold any single study loosely.)
What strong teachers of Black students do

Gloria Ladson-Billings studied successful teachers of African American students and found that they held high expectations, validated students' cultural identities, and treated differences as assets. She named three pillars of **culturally relevant teaching** (Ladson-Billings, 1995):

columns: What it sounds like in a classroom
rows: "I expect you to do this work, and I will not let you coast. Here is the support."
A teacher uses a student's neighborhood, language, or family tradition as a way into the lesson, and students do not have to leave their identity at the door.
Students learn to ask who benefits from the way something is, and they use their learning to take on real problems in their communities.

blocks.description: The researcher behind the Pygmalion study explains what he found and what he thinks it means for classrooms.

blocks.description: Ladson-Billings talks through what culturally relevant teaching looks like in practice. Good if you want to hear the idea in her own voice.

blocks.text: **Deficit thinking** focuses on what is wrong with a student, a family, or a community: what they lack, cannot do, or do not have. It rarely sounds hostile. More often it sounds tired, practical, or even caring.
It shows up in three places:

items: **Language.** Phrases like "those kids," "at-risk," and "low" describe a child by a label, not by what the child knows.
**Policy.** Tracking systems limit access to rigorous content, and discipline policies exclude Black, brown, and low-income students at higher rates.
**Practice.** A teacher plans a simpler task for a group of students before checking what they can already do.

blocks.text: The language adults use matters well beyond one conversation. It shapes the beliefs other adults hold, and over time it shapes the beliefs students hold about themselves. The shift is a change in the question you ask: from *"What is wrong with this student?"* to *"What does this student know, and how do I build on it?"*

blocks.title: A reframe is not a spin
blocks.text: Asset-based language still names real needs. "He is a low reader" and "He decodes accurately, loves nonfiction, and needs support with fluency" describe the same child; the second tells you what to do on Monday.
Try it: reframe it
Read each statement, decide how you would reframe it, then reveal one possible version. Not graded.

items.reveal: He decodes accurately, loves nonfiction, and needs support with fluency.

blocks.text: When some families seem distant from school, it is easy to read that as not caring. The research says otherwise. Skepticism toward schools among historically underserved families is a response to institutional failure, and it comes from families who care deeply about their children's education (Ladson-Billings, 2017). Studies consistently find that Black and low-income families are deeply invested in education and see school as one of the most reliable pathways to opportunity.

Asset-based family engagement treats parents and caregivers as **experts on their own children** and as partners in the work. KIPP DC's mission begins with the words "Together with families and communities," and that is a structural commitment, not a slogan.
Belief shows up in action

items: **Start with listening.** Make your first contact a question, such as "What should I know about your child?" and not a report.
**Offer more than one way in.** Try calls, texts, notes home, and in-person moments, and ask each family what works best.
**Share good news early.** A family whose first call is a positive one will pick up the next call.

blocks.text: Share strengths first and growth second
Use plain words a family can use at home. Skip jargon and labels.

rows: "Maya is below grade level in reading and needs intervention."
"Maya reads aloud with expression; next we are working on finishing her sentences. At home, you can ask her to read you one page and tell you what happened."
"Jaylen has great ideas and speaks up quickly. We are practicing waiting for a teammate to finish before he adds his."

blocks.text: Use what families tell you

What a family shares about their child, routines, and goals is **information**, not a favor. Use it to shape seating, grouping, communication, and the supports you offer. A parent who says her son is up late helping with a younger sibling has just told you something about when to schedule his hardest work.

blocks.title: Engaging Families Through Home Visits
blocks.description: A recorded webinar on building relationships with families by starting from their expertise. The home-visit model is one of several ways to make a first contact.

blocks.text: Everyone brings a **cultural lens** shaped by their own background, and that lens shapes what they notice and expect. You are not a blank slate, and neither is any teacher. Naming your lens is not a confession; it is a professional skill.
Engaging respectfully across difference comes down to three habits: **ask before assuming**, **learn from families and communities**, and **check generalizations** against the person in front of you.

You already thought about this in Section 2. Norms for participation, such as eye contact, personal space, and turn-taking, vary across cultures. A student who looks down or waits before speaking may be showing respect or thinking carefully, not disengaging. The first move is a question, not a conclusion.

blocks.prompt: Think of a time you misread someone because of your own lens. What did you assume, and what would have helped you check?

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes an asset-based approach to teaching?

options.text: Celebrating cultural differences during designated heritage months while maintaining standard instruction
Avoiding any acknowledgment of academic gaps so students do not feel discouraged
Focusing on what students know and can do, and building instruction from those strengths
Lowering academic expectations so that all students can experience success

questions.explanation: Asset-based teaching starts from students' strengths and builds instruction from them, without lowering expectations.

questions.prompt: What does Rosenthal and Jacobson's 1968 Pygmalion research demonstrate about teacher expectations?

options.text: Students tend to rise or fall to the level of belief their teacher holds about them, regardless of their actual starting point
Positive expectations only benefit students who already have a strong academic foundation
Only the expectations of highly experienced teachers influence student performance
Teacher expectations have no measurable impact on student outcomes once students reach middle school

questions.explanation: The Pygmalion Effect shows that teacher beliefs shape student outcomes, whatever the starting point.

questions.prompt: A teacher looks at a student's cumulative file before the year begins and thinks, "This student has a lot of absences and low test scores. This is going to be a challenging year." Which of the following best describes this kind of thinking?

options.text: Neutral: reviewing records is standard practice and does not reflect a mindset
Deficit thinking: the teacher is starting with what the student lacks rather than what they bring
Culturally relevant: the teacher is using data to inform their instruction
Asset-based: the teacher is being realistic about the student's needs

questions.explanation: Starting from what a student lacks, before meeting them, is deficit thinking.

questions.prompt: According to Ladson-Billings' research, what do effective teachers of Black students consistently do?

options.text: Avoid discussing race and culture in class to maintain a neutral environment
Hold high expectations, validate students' cultural identities, and view student differences as assets
Focus exclusively on academic content and leave cultural competence to other staff
Lower expectations to reduce stress and build confidence gradually

questions.explanation: Effective teachers pair high expectations with cultural validation and see differences as assets.

questions.prompt: A parent misses a school event and doesn't respond to a teacher's phone call. Which response reflects an asset-based approach to families?

options.text: "I've done my part. It's up to them to show up."
"This family is clearly not invested in their child's education."
"I should report this to administration so they can follow up."
"I'll try a different way of reaching out. They may have barriers I don't know about, and they deserve my effort."

questions.explanation: An asset-based response assumes good intent, considers barriers, and keeps reaching out.
